actions.purpose: Compare O-ring thermal distress against joint temperature across all prior flights, including flights without distress.

assumptions.proposition: The Commission's GMT event table (General Purpose Computer time) is the reference for flight event times.

causes.mechanism: PHYSICAL MECHANISM: a field joint design unacceptably sensitive to temperature, dimensions, materials, reuse, processing and joint rotation (root cause) failed to seal at or shortly after ignition when cold-stiffened O-rings in a tight gap probably could not follow the opening joint (trigger); hot gas leaked, reappeared as a plume at about 58 s, breached the External Tank and led to the structural breakup at about 73 s. ORGANIZATIONAL CONTRIBUTING CAUSE (not part of the physical mechanism): the decision to launch was flawed; Thiokol management reversed its engineers' recommendation at Marshall's urging, the concern appears to have been contained below Levels I and II, safety was absent, and erosion had for years been accepted as flight risk (contributing factors), with schedule pressure as an enabling condition. The organizational weighting follows Rogers Ch. V and VI; the House Committee places years of poor technical decision-making above communication, recorded as an accepted contradiction.
causes.outcome: Loss of Challenger 73 seconds after launch on 28 January 1986

conclusions.residualUncertainty: Accepted residuals: the exact joint temperature (28 +/- 5, about 50, 31 and about 8 degrees F measure different positions and quantities); whether the leak was continuous or resealed between 3 and 58 s; whether informing Levels I and II would have changed the outcome (Rogers 'seems likely ... might not', House 'no evidence'); the House Committee's heavier weighting of long-term technical decision-making over communication; conflicting participant testimony about the teleconference. Several Commission findings used here are hedged ('probable', 'appears', 'apparently'). Joint verification rests on ground firings plus one warm-weather flight assessed by the contractor; STS-26 flew before QM-8 completed its qualification set; the vent valves may have failed before launch, letting water into the joints (STS-26-M-2); vent-port-plug O-rings were damaged in assembly and heater sensors were misconnected. The CAIB finding is later (2003) knowledge from a primary investigation report, not available in 1988. The safety-office and flight-rate preventions are recorded as implemented or approved but are not verified here.
conclusions.statement: Challenger was lost because the pressure seal in the aft field joint of the right Solid Rocket Motor failed at or shortly after ignition: a joint design unacceptably sensitive to temperature and other factors probably could not seal with cold-stiffened O-rings (modelled at 28 +/- 5 degrees F at the coldest point) in a tight, strut-loaded gap. Separately, and as a contributing cause rather than part of the physical mechanism, the decision to launch was flawed: Thiokol's engineering recommendation against launching below 53 degrees F was reversed by management at Marshall's urging and did not reach the final decision makers, within a program that had for years accepted O-ring erosion as flight risk. The redesigned field joint completed its full-scale test set, sealed without field-joint erosion or blow-by on STS-26 and was certified with heated joints in a cold-conditioned motor (QM-8). The institutional correction was not effective: in 2003 the Columbia Accident Investigation Board found the institutional causes of Challenger had not been fixed.

contradictions.basis: Accepted as residual: STS-26 flew outside the full committed qualification set; the set was completed by QM-8 before the third flight (CH-C108).
contradictions.statement: The June 1987 plan committed to three qualification firings before the next flight; only two preceded STS-26, and the cold-conditioned QM-8 was fired in January 1989, after the flight.

contradictions.basis: Both are recorded: the erosion history was briefed and available, but it was not treated as a constraint on launch, and the 27 January engineering objection did not reach the final decision makers. The decision hypothesis is stated in those terms.
contradictions.statement: The Commission's Ch. V finding says decision makers were unaware of the recent O-ring history, while the House Committee and Rogers Ch. VI Finding 5 say the history was presented to all levels, including Level I at Headquarters in August 1985.

contradictions.basis: The two bodies disagree on a counterfactual that no evidence can settle; both agree the decision process was flawed (CH-C040, CH-C084). Preserved as residual uncertainty.
contradictions.statement: The Rogers Commission judged that had decision makers known all the facts it is highly unlikely they would have launched; the House Committee found no evidence the outcome would have differed had Levels I and II been informed.

contradictions.basis: A difference of emphasis between the two investigating bodies. The causal roles follow Rogers Ch. V and VI (long-term acceptance of erosion as a contributing factor alongside the decision factors); the House weighting, which ranks years of poor technical decision-making first, is preserved here as an accepted contradiction rather than resolved.
contradictions.statement: The House Committee placed weight on Thiokol's failure over many flight readiness reviews to establish a minimum temperature, and on years of poor technical decision-making, rather than on the 27 January communication failure.

contradictions.basis: The primary Commission text governs; the secondary wording is a popular simplification and is not used as a finding.
contradictions.statement: A secondary NASA history article says the O-rings 'became brittle' and the External Tank 'exploded'; the Commission's findings describe loss of resiliency and a structural failure with an explosive burn of propellants.

contradictions.statement: Mulloy denied pressing Thiokol to reconsider its data, while the Commission found Thiokol reversed its position at the urging of Marshall.

contradictions.basis: Every estimate for the 300-degree region of the joint, and the ambient value, is below the 53 degrees F of the coldest previous flight; the causal conclusion does not depend on which estimate is used. The values measure different things and are kept as stated.
contradictions.statement: The 51-L joint temperature differs by source, position and what is measured: 28 +/- 5 degrees F modelled at the coldest point, about 50 degrees F on the sun-facing side, 31 degrees F in the Figure 2 table, about 8 degrees F from a pyrometer on the right SRB surface, and 36 degrees F ambient.

contradictions.basis: Recollections given months later conflict on wording and tone; four witnesses (Boisjoly, Lund, Mason, McDonald) reported Hardy's 'appalled' remark and Lund testified to Marshall's rejection (CH-C087, CH-C121). The documented sequence of recommendation, caucus and reversal is not in dispute.
contradictions.statement: Participants' accounts of the 27 January teleconferences conflict: whether Thiokol recommended delay at 5:45 p.m., Hardy's 'appalled' remark, the 'next April' remark, the tone of the Thiokol caucus and McDonald's interjection.

correctiveActions.description: Set a flight rate consistent with resources and avoid reliance on a single launch capability (Recommendation VIII).

Redesign the Solid Rocket Motor field joint (Commission Recommendation I): tang capture feature, third O-ring, J-seal insulation and joint heaters that keep seal temperatures at or above 75 degrees F; test and certify it full scale.

Strengthen flight readiness and launch-decision communication: recorded FRR and Mission Management Team meetings, crew commander attendance, launch constraints approved and waived only by the Director, NSTS (Recommendation V).
Establish an independent Office of Safety, Reliability, Maintainability and Quality Assurance under an Associate Administrator (Recommendation IV).

criteria.expectedOutcome: The institutional causes of the flawed launch decision, including the flight readiness review process, are corrected so that they do not recur, as judged at the next independent review of the Shuttle program (the Columbia Accident Investigation Board, 2003).
criteria.method: Later independent investigation of the Shuttle program

criteria.expectedOutcome: On the return-to-flight mission the redesigned field joints seal without blow-by or erosion, as shown by a primary post-flight inspection record.
criteria.method: Primary post-flight SRM inspection record for STS-26

criteria.expectedOutcome: The redesigned joint system (seals held warm by field-joint heaters) is certified in a cold-conditioned full-scale motor before any cold-weather launch.

The redesigned motor completes its committed full-scale test set - development, qualification (including cold-conditioned) and production verification firings, including tests with intentional joint flaws.
criteria.method: Full-scale static firings reported in NASA and contractor documentation

findings.interpretation: The comparison the launch-decision meeting did not make supports a temperature effect; the cold sample is small (four flights), so it is supporting rather than conclusive evidence.
findings.originalResult: Rogers Commission Ch. VI (joint temperature): including all flights, all four flights at 63 degrees F or below had O-ring distress, against three of twenty at 66 degrees F or above; managers on 27 January compared only the flights with distress [CH-C056]. (Ch. IV Finding 12 gives the same pattern by ambient temperature with a 61 degree F threshold [CH-C024].)

history.reason: Levels I and II did not know of the launch constraint or its waivers.
Commission Finding 3 ('appears to be a propensity') and testimony that senior officials did not know of the 27 January objections; the House Committee disputes the weight of this factor.

hypotheses.statement: Marshall management appears to have contained the O-ring concern within the project instead of communicating it to Levels I and II (the Commission's Finding 3 is worded 'appears to be a propensity').

history.reason: Thiokol engineers recommended no launch below 53 degrees F; management reversed after a caucus.
Commission Finding 4: the reversal was at Marshall's urging and contrary to the engineers.

hypotheses.statement: Thiokol management reversed its engineers' no-launch recommendation at the urging of Marshall to accommodate a major customer.

history.reason: The Commission found no other element or the payload contributed and sabotage was not a factor.

hypotheses.statement: Another Shuttle element, the payload, or sabotage caused or contributed to the joint leak.

history.reason: Photographic data place the first smoke at the right SRB aft field joint at 0.678 s.
The Commission and the House Committee both conclude the aft field joint seal of the right SRM failed because of a faulty design.

hypotheses.mechanism: The field joint design was unacceptably sensitive to temperature, physical dimensions, character of materials, reusability, processing and the reaction of the joint to dynamic loading (CH-C016); a leak initiated at or shortly after ignition (CH-C017), reappeared as flame at about 58 s (CH-C026) and impinged on the External Tank (CH-C009, CH-C010).
hypotheses.statement: The faulty design of the right Solid Rocket Motor aft field joint caused the pressure seal to fail, letting combustion gas leak and weaken and/or penetrate the External Tank.

history.reason: Decision makers were unaware of the O-ring history and of the engineers' opposition.
The Commission found a serious flaw in the decision-making process; it judged that with clearly stated concerns the launch 'might not have occurred when it did'.

hypotheses.mechanism: Commission Ch. V finding and Finding 1 (CH-C027, CH-C040); the Commission's counterfactual is hedged: 'it seems likely that the launch of 51-L might not have occurred when it did' (CH-C114). The history was available at all levels (CH-C110, CH-C111); what was not passed on was the 27 January objection.
hypotheses.statement: The launch decision process was flawed: Thiokol's initial recommendation against launch and the continuing opposition of its engineers did not reach those who made the final decision, and the O-ring erosion history, although briefed to Level I in August 1985, was not acted on as a constraint on launch.

history.reason: Launch ambient temperature was 15 degrees F colder than any previous launch.
Resiliency tests, the joint temperature estimate, the gap and strut findings and the all-flights distress comparison agree; the Commission states the sealing failure as probable, not certain.

hypotheses.mechanism: O-ring resiliency falls with temperature (CH-C021); at the launch temperature the O-ring would 'probably' not be pressure-actuated in time to preclude blow-by (CH-C022); the gap was at most .008 in and on average .004 in (CH-C019), and with a .004 in gap sealing is marginal even at 40-50 degrees F (CH-C023); the 310-degree strut enhanced gap opening by 10-20 percent at 300-320 degrees (CH-C124); putty delay could be a factor (CH-C125). Other joints had similar gap and temperature combinations (CH-C126), so cold alone does not explain why this joint failed. Smoke appeared at 0.678 s (CH-C005).
hypotheses.statement: At ignition the O-rings, their resiliency reduced by cold (modelled at 28 +/- 5 degrees F at the coldest point of the joint), combined with a tight tang-to-clevis gap and strut-enhanced joint opening near the 300-degree position, probably could not follow the opening gap quickly enough to seal, so blow-by and erosion began at or shortly after ignition.

history.reason: No safety representative was at the teleconference or on the Mission Management Team.
Little or no trend analysis of O-ring erosion and blow-by was performed.

hypotheses.statement: The safety, reliability and quality assurance organization was silent: absent from the launch-decision forums and doing little or no trend analysis of O-ring distress.

history.reason: Erosion was accepted as acceptable risk after 51-C.
Waivers, accepted erosion and unheeded warnings over the preceding years; the House Committee names years of poor technical decision-making as the fundamental problem.

hypotheses.statement: Over the preceding years NASA and Thiokol accepted escalating O-ring erosion and blow-by as an acceptable flight risk, apparently because earlier flights had survived it, waiving launch constraints and relying on flight-readiness rationales (later literature calls this normalization; the 1986 sources say 'acceptable risk').

history.reason: The scheduled flight rate left no margin for unforeseen hardware problems.
Rogers Ch. VIII (hedged) and the House Committee finding that schedule pressure contributed to unsafe launch operations.

hypotheses.statement: Pressure to meet an ambitious flight rate left no margin for unforeseen hardware problems and may have obscured engineering concerns (Rogers hedges this: 'may occasionally'; the House Committee finds it directly contributed to unsafe launch operations).

history.reason: The Commission found pad ice was not a cause of the accident.

hypotheses.statement: Ice on the launch pad or vehicle struck the Orbiter or SRB and caused the failure.

history.reason: The Commission states only that water may have been in the clevis.
Possible, not established: the Commission's finding is conditional ('may have been'), so ice is not part of the established cause.

hypotheses.statement: Water that froze in the right aft field joint clevis inhibited the secondary seal.

observations.original: The flight ended 73 seconds after launch in an explosive burn of hydrogen and oxygen propellants that destroyed the External Tank; aerodynamic loads caused complete structural breakup of the Orbiter and all seven crew members perished. [CH-C002]
The Mission Management Team scrubbed the 27 January launch at 12:36 p.m. due to high cross winds; the following discussion produced no SRB constraints for a 9:38 a.m. launch on 28 January. [CH-C030]
At 0.678 s MET, photographic data show a strong puff of gray smoke from the vicinity of the right SRB aft field joint (E60 camera; 16:38:00.688 GMT). [CH-C005]
Phase 2 of the teleconference commenced at approximately 8:45 p.m. EST after Thiokol charts arrived by telefax. [CH-C032]
At about 5:00 a.m. on 28 January Mulloy told Lucas only that Thiokol temperature concerns had been resolved in favor of launch. [CH-C046]
Kilminster requested a five-minute off-net caucus that lasted about 30 minutes; the teleconference recessed at about 10:30 p.m. EST. [CH-C034]
The first visual indication that flame breached the External Tank was at 64.660 s MET (abrupt plume shape/color change indicating leaking hydrogen). [CH-C010]
The range safety system destructed the right SRB at 110.250 s MET (39:50.260 GMT) and the left at 110.252 s. [CH-C123]
At about 72.20 s the lower strut linking the right SRB and External Tank was severed or pulled away from the weakened hydrogen tank, letting the right SRB rotate around the upper strut. [CH-C122]
Chronology: Thiokol (Lund) recommended not flying 51-L until O-ring temperature reached 53 degrees F, the lowest of any previous flight; Kilminster said he could not recommend launch. [CH-C033]
Eight more puffs of increasingly blacker smoke were recorded between 0.836 and 2.500 s MET. [CH-C007]
At about 11 p.m. EST the teleconference resumed; Thiokol management said temperature effects were a concern but data inconclusive, and Kilminster read the rationale recommending launch. [CH-C037]
Mulloy testified that in the ~11:30 p.m. call to Aldrich about recovery-area weather he did not discuss the Thiokol conversations, regarding it as a resolved Level III issue. [CH-C045]
At 73.124 s MET a circumferential white vapor pattern on the External Tank aft dome marked the beginning of hydrogen tank structural failure. [CH-C011]
Ambient air temperature at launch was 36 degrees F, measured at ground level about 1,000 feet from pad 39B, 15 degrees colder than any previous launch. [CH-C004]
The flame became a continuous, well-defined plume at 59.262 s; at about 60 s telemetry showed right SRB chamber pressure lower than the left. [CH-C009]
Challenger mission 51-L began its flight at 11:38 a.m. EST on 28 January 1986. [CH-C001]
The last validated Orbiter telemetry measurement was at 73.618 s MET (16:39:13.628 GMT). [CH-C013]
SRM ignition command (T=0) occurred at 16:38:00.010 GMT per General Purpose Computer data. [CH-C003]

Historical investigation recorded from primary sources. Challenger mission 51-L began its flight at 11:38 a.m. EST on 28 January 1986; the flight ended 73 seconds after launch when the External Tank was destroyed and the Orbiter broke up [CH-C001, CH-C002]. Scope: the physical failure and the organizational decision to launch, kept separate as the Rogers Commission keeps them.
The first very small flame on the right SRB near the aft field joint was detected on image-enhanced film at 58.788 s MET (E207 camera; 16:38:58.798 GMT), at about 305 degrees circumference. [CH-C008]

The first phase of the Marshall-Thiokol teleconference began at 5:45 p.m. EST on 27 January. The Commission narrative says Thiokol presented low-temperature concerns "along with an opinion that launch should be delayed"; this point is contested in testimony (CH-C085). [CH-C031]

Ice crew infrared pyrometer readings (7:00-9:00 a.m. EST) showed the left SRB at about 25 degrees F and the right SRB at about 8 degrees F near the aft region; not reported since no LCC covered surface temperatures. [CH-C047]
Hardy requested the Thiokol recommendation in writing by telefax to Kennedy and Marshall, and it was sent; the chronology places a Kilminster-signed fax at about 11:45 p.m. EST. [CH-C038]
The intertank and lower liquid oxygen tank structures failed at 73.137 s MET. [CH-C012]
